## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of cross-lane bit manipulation and wrap-around across a 128-bit value.

## Key Concepts
- 128-bit split across two uint64 halves
- Cross-lane bit movement with shifts
- Non-branching bitwise updates

## Code Example

```c
uint128 rotateLeft128_1(uint128 x) {
  uint64_t new_lo = (x.lo << 1) | (x.hi >> 63);
  uint64_t new_hi = (x.hi << 1) | (x.lo >> 63);
  uint128 r; r.hi = new_hi; r.lo = new_lo; return r;
}
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Question Matters
Tests the ability to implement bitwise rotation on 128-bit words without branches, while safely handling edge cases.

## Key Concepts
- **Bitwise rotation**: Moves bits cyclically; bits shifted out one end re-enter from the other.
- **Safe shift masking**: The `k &= 127` constrains k to [0, 127], preventing undefined behavior when k >= word width.
- **No loops or conditionals**: Shift and OR operations execute in constant time for low-latency systems.

## Code Breakdown
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 127;                    // mask to valid range
  return (x << k) | (x >> (128 - k));  // rotate via split-shift-OR
}
```
- `(x << k)` moves the high bits toward the left, discarding overflow.
- `(x >> (128 - k))` captures the bits that "wrap around" to the right.
- OR combines both halves into a single cyclic result.

## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of bit tricks and boundary handling for 32-bit values. Rotations require combining shifted parts without branching.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation using shifts
- Modulo behavior for bit widths
- Signed vs unsigned handling in C/JS contexts

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotl32(n, k) {
  k = k & 31; // 0..31
  return ((n << k) | (n >>> (32 - k))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you implement rotl64 in C for uint64_t, ensuring performance on common compilers?
- Could you map this to intrinsic functions (e.g., __builtin_rotate) on supported platforms?

## Why This Is Asked
Endianness is a practical concern in systems and networking. This question tests precise bit-twiddling with masks and shifts, without relying on loops. It also checks understanding of how a 32-bit word maps to byte positions.

## Key Concepts
- Byte extraction with masks
- Shifting to relocate bytes
- Endianness awareness and portability
- No loops; pure bitwise operations

## Code Example
```c
uint32_t swapEndian32(uint32_t n) {
  return (n >> 24) | ((n >> 8) & 0x0000FF00) | ((n << 8) & 0x00FF0000) | (n << 24);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit values?
- How would you implement an endianness swap for 16-bit values or for an array of 32-bit words efficiently?

## Why This Is Asked
This tests the ability to implement a branchless, 64-bit rotate using masking and shifts—a fundamental low-level technique in performance-critical code.

## Key Concepts
- 64-bit masking with &63 to constrain the rotation range
- Branchless rotation via (n >> r) | (n << (64 - r))
- Edge-case handling for k=0 without conditional branches

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateRight64(n, k) {
  const r = k & 63;
  return (n >>> r) | (n << ((64 - r) & 63));
}
```

## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests understanding of 128-bit shifts, wrap-around logic, and edge cases where n==0. Requires a clean, branch-minimal implementation without loops.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation across 128 bits
- Handling edge cases safely (n==0, 128-n)
- Avoiding undefined shifts across boundary bits

## Code Example
```c
uint128 rotateLeft128(uint128 x, uint8 n) {
  n &= 127;
  if (n == 0) return x;
  return (x << n) | (x >> (128 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for a language without 128-bit integers?
- How would compiler optimizations affect this implementation in real code?
